clusters.title_hint: NASA Explores Potential Commercial Servicing for Hubble Telescope

sources.title: NASA Explores Potential Commercial Servicing for Hubble Telescope
sources.text:
NASA issued a Request for Information Oct. 29 to learn more about industry capabilities for in-space servicing to support the agency’s Hubble Space Telescope.
“Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe.”
The Request for Information seeks commercial interest in: potentially conducting a mission to boost Hubble to a higher altitude to extend its science lifetime; servicing Hubble to enhance its capabilities; or performing a safe, controlled re-entry into Earth’s atmosphere or orbital disposal at the end of Hubble’s mission.
“Hubble is a national icon that has fundamentally changed how humanity views our universe for more than 35 years,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “Commercial industry has rapidly evolved in recent years to offer new capabilities for in-space satellite capture and servicing. Given the time we have until Hubble’s anticipated re-entry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow.”
The Request for Information is available online and will remain open for responses until 3 p.m. EST, Monday, Nov. 30.
Like all spacecraft in low Earth orbit, Hubble’s altitude is slowly decreasing over time because of atmospheric drag. Hubble does not have a propulsion system to maintain its own orbit, and analysis predicts Hubble is likely to re-enter the atmosphere in the 2033 to 2034 timeframe. As such, NASA anticipates that a mission would need to take place by 2032.
The Hubble Space Telescope has been operating for more than three decades and continues to make ground-breaking discoveries that shape our fundamental understanding of the universe. Hubble is a project of international cooperation between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency). NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, manages the telescope and mission operations. Lockheed Martin Space, based in Denver, also supports mission operations at Goddard. The Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, conducts Hubble science operations for NASA.

sources.title: Think you can save the Hubble Space Telescope? NASA wants to know.
sources.text:
The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century.
NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction.
The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance through, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry.

If you’ve been waiting for a good deal on Google’s latest smartwatch before you commit, you're in luck. The Google Pixel Watch 5 (the 41-mm model with Wi-Fi) is currently $300, down from $400, marking its lowest price yet. (The larger 45-mm model is also discounted, from $430 to $330.)
This early Black Friday sale means you don’t have to wait until the late-November holiday to score the worthwhile discount—and we recommend you don't. Amazon, Best Buy, and the Google Store are all offering the 25 percent off deal, but I don't know for how much longer. In other words, now is a great time to score this smartwatch for less.
A Record-Low Price
The Pixel Watch 5 is one of the best smartwatches available for Android users. It’s a refinement of an already brilliant wearable, with double the RAM and storage, plus an upgraded Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 processor that makes this edition 20 percent faster than its predecessor. The domed display is gorgeous, comfortable, and easy to read during workouts, and it provides meaningful upgrades for health and fitness tracking.
Beyond being able to track weights and reps, the new Strength Training experience includes a workout builder, audio cues, and rest times. You can build a custom routine in the Google Health app and have the watch guide you through each exercise, and incorporate Gemini AI by asking it to generate a workout based on a photo of your gym equipment. Speaking of Gemini, the Pixel Watch 5 supports certain offline tasks, such as starting a workout, which is nice if you like to leave your watch at home while you exercise.
Google’s new Health Guardian tools include features for monitoring insulin resistance trends, blood pressure trends, breathing emergencies (available only in select countries), and sleep breathing quality. The watch also retains useful features like ECG, skin temperature tracking, and loss-of-pulse detection. It comes with upgraded sleep tracking, too, with Google claiming 15 percent greater accuracy than the Pixel Watch 4.
Google estimates up to 40 hours of battery life, but mine only got to around 36 hours in testing before conking out. Fast charging is the real standout, though; just 15 minutes on the charger delivers up to 15 hours of use. If you’re like me and only remember to charge your watch 20 minutes before leaving the house, this is a lifesaver.
At its original $400 price, the Pixel Watch 5 is a pricey recommendation, especially since many of its software upgrades will also make their way to the previous generation. But at $300, it’s cheaper than the latest Apple Watch Series 12 and other high-end smartwatches. This is the lowest price I’ve seen for the Pixel Watch 5, so if you’ve been eyeing it, there’s little reason to wait for Black Friday.

sources.title: Martin Scorsese Says His ‘Cleopatra’ Movie With Angelina Jolie Was ‘Ruined’ by Seth Rogen and the Sony Hack: ‘It Was Gonna Be Really Wild’
sources.text:
Martin Scorsese‘s “Cleopatra” never came to fruition, and he says the Angelina Jolie-starrer was nixed because of Seth Rogen and the Sony hack.
For those who need a refresher, Sony emails were hacked in November 2014 by a group that hoped the Seth Rogen comedy “The Interview,” which was about a fictional assassination attempt of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, would not be released by Sony.
According to Scorsese, this caused some aftereffects in the industry, which he described in the first episode of the Tribeca original series “Crafty.”
“We were gonna do Cleopatra at one point, and then they made fun of [Kim Jong Un], and he got mad and blew up everybody at Columbia,” Scorsese said. “Seth Rogen, right? And then he got mad, and [it] ruined Cleopatra.”
Though Rogen wasn’t directly responsible for the project being canceled, the resulting hack exposed thousands of emails, including ones from producer Scott Rudin to Sony’s Amy Pascal calling Jolie “a minimally talented spoiled brat.”
“We were gonna do it,” Scorsese also said. “Angelina Jolie. We were going. She was gonna be Cleopatra VII. It was gonna be really wild.”
The film was set to be written by screenwriter Eric Roth, who wrote Scorsese’s 2023 film “Killers of the Flower Moon.”

sources.title: LAPD Arrests 2 Men In Connection With Killing Of ‘SNL’ Writer Jimmy Fowlie’s Sister
sources.text:
Nearly a year after she went missing, LAPD has arrested two men in connection to the death of Christina Downer, the late sister of Saturday Night Live writer Jimmy Fowlie.
On Thursday, officers took 41-year-old Delorean Bijon Brandon, who is believed to be Downer’s boyfriend, and Kaylee Markowski, 34, into custody for allegedly murdering and disposing of her body, before concealing their involvement.
Brandon and Markowski are both being held at Metropolitan Detention Center, where they have been booked on suspicion of murder and are both being held on $2 million bail.
According to LAPD, Brandon claimed Downer had moved out of their home several months before her disappearance, leaving behind all of her belongings, including her vehicle and dog.
Watch on Deadline
Downer’s family reported her missing on Dec. 18, 2025, following a welfare check requested by her ex-husband after he hadn’t heard from her in an extended period of time. Detectives with LAPD’s Robbery-Homicide Division took over the investigation when her cellphone was discovered washed ashore on a Santa Monica beach.
Last December, Fowlie sought help from friends and followers as he searched Downer’s Koreatown neighborhood, noting they were “worried that she isn’t safe.” Fowlie announced in April that LAPD had informed the family that Downer was “no longer alive,” and were treating the case as a homicide.

clusters.title_hint: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals

sources.title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals
sources.text:
While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens.
Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI.
Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on.
The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies.
“As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.”
Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold.
At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI, a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther, a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS.
Nexus, a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. The system can handle 2.4 terabits per second on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with inference running on premises, next to the instrument.
Put together, the system enables an agent to steer a telescope’s antennae, calibrate and focus the instrument for a clean signal, catch and fix data errors and plot the result. Agents compress what would take humans weeks or years into hours.
The pipeline has already proven itself, achieving the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar — a rapidly spinning stellar remnant that pulses like a cosmic lighthouse — in the Crab Nebula.
Next, the team is evaluating open models including NVIDIA Nemotron for cases where data locality and turnaround matter most and for observatories that may someday run offline on the far side of the moon.

The brief ceremony introducing the new Macbook Pro this week was as low-key as the presenter, Apple’s new CEO John Ternus. He stepped onto the low stage at a Los Angeles event space with zero fanfare, said hi, and queued up a video showing the first touchscreen Mac. Then he released the modest crowd of journalists and creators to get hands-on with the new laptop and roam between eye-popping demos of music producers, filmmakers, photographers, and fashion designers using the laptop. Ternus, who at 51 is on the younger side of Apple’s top management, has been CEO for less than two months. But this launch and a series of other recent announcements have made one thing clear. With this new guy—if a 25-year Apple veteran could be considered new—it’s all about the products. Perhaps fittingly, the biggest noise of the presentation came when Ternus revealed that the new device restores the illumination to the Apple logo. Maybe that’s a symbol that in the age of AI, Apple is beaming out the message that hardware still rules.
A few minutes after the presentation, I sat down with Ternus, for the second time in two days. Steve Jobs used to grant me an audience after his famous keynotes, too. Ternus isn’t Jobs, of course, nor is he supposed to be. But who is he?
I first met Ternus in 2015, when I spent a day with him at Apple’s Input Design Lab, a testing facility in Cupertino. He’d risen to VP for Mac, iPad, Ecosystem, and Audio Engineering, and he struck me as affable and knowledgeable. (He spent four years right out of college at a virtual reality company, but he’s been at Apple ever since.) The peg to my story at the time was how this unknown manager conducted a Javert-like investigation to fix the weird sound a redesigned mouse made when sliding on a table.
That attention to detail was a legacy of Jobs’ perfectionism, which Tim Cook sustained as the next CEO. In the decade when Ternus overlapped with Jobs, he says he had only “a handful of interactions” with the founder. “But I've always felt like sort of a student of Steve's teachings,” Ternus said. “And then being able to work very closely with Tim, I’ve been very lucky.”
Ternus has so far been defined by his product prowess. “John innately has a great sense for great products, and that’s what Apple is,” says Greg Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of worldwide marketing and a 40-year company veteran. “You can’t teach that.” In one sense Ternus’ ascension is similar to that of Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, another lifer promoted to the top post. But Nadella was called upon to fix a broken organization, while Apple has been on a multi-decade run. Ternus is explicit that he will be an engine of continuity. That word is key to his selection, and above all explains why Tim Cook and the rest of Apple’s board was so comfortable with the choice.
The extent to which Ternus is a deep Apple insider became clear when I probed him on his views on being a corporate leader. I asked him which non-Apple CEOs he admires, and he was stumped. “I haven't really thought about that,” he said. I asked whether any business books had an impact on him. “Not really,” he said. “Of course I’ve read books, but there's so much to be learned from the people I get to work with.” Indeed, every time I tried to pin down Ternus on what mark he wants to make at Apple, he deflected the question and told me how he will continue Apple’s commitment to internal collaboration.
Ternus’ key collaborator is probably Johny Srouji, the architect of the company’s custom silicon, an initiative that’s driven many of the company’s innovations in the past decade. sources.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
sources.text:
Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.
Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.
Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.
Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation.
David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes.
Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection.
Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries.
Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator.
The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error.
The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing.
Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene (ovstage), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments.
With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin, developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows.
Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments.
For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment.
Find assets in SimReady Central Library, and learn how to contribute.
A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene.
When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns.
Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling.
With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements.
Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve.

clusters.title_hint: NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found

sources.title: NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found
sources.text:
5 min read
When a rose-colored meteorite was found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, no one knew how old it was or where it came from. Not until NASA-funded scientists age-dated its minerals did they realize the nearly 2-pound (800-gram) rock was a piece of Mars that formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one of the oldest Martian meteorites ever found. Named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered, the meteorite is one of roughly 435 from the Red Planet.
In a paper published Thursday in Science, researchers offered an initial characterization of Teghaza 001, providing a rare snapshot of Mars’ ancient crust and formation. What scientists learn from future studies could help answer many questions, including how water and rocks interacted on ancient Mars. A separate paper published in Science Advances in June detailed the meteorite’s water content, offering a look at how water shaped the early planet’s surface.
“It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique,” said the paper’s lead author, Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars.”
What sets Teghaza 001 apart from other Martian meteorites is its texture and age as well as the uniqueness of its igneous, or volcanic, minerals. It is one of the three most ancient Martian meteorites found on Earth. While invaluable, the others provide more limited glimpses of Mars’ geological history. They include ALH84001, which is composed almost entirely of one mineral and is similar in age to Teghaza 001. The other meteorite, nicknamed “Black Beauty,” formed about 2.1 billion years ago and is composed of small, volcanic rock fragments.
Unlike its ancient peers, Teghaza 001 has a mix of igneous minerals that tells a story about how the planet’s crust formed from cooling magma before it was eventually altered by subsurface water. The meteorite’s distinctive mineralogy matches what NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter has observed in the planet’s cratered southern highlands. No one will ever know exactly where the meteorite originated on Mars, but the paper identifies several potential locations that match Teghaza 001’s mineralogy and chemistry.
“This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before,” said the new paper’s second author, Lee Saper, who conducted the research while at JPL as a postdoctoral scholar. Lee now is a scientist at NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley. “It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water.”
Although the Mars meteorites found on Earth differ from one another, they share a common history, having been blasted off the Red Planet’s surface by an impact, followed by a trajectory that eventually placed them on Earth and into the hands of scientists. Meteorites are often found by collectors in deserts or snowy plains, where they stand out from the rest of the barren landscape. Scientists can verify a meteorite as Martian by matching its mineral and chemical components to data collected by NASA’s Mars missions, including the Viking landers as well as the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers.
When Liu was first asked to look at Teghaza 001, she almost passed on the opportunity.
Researchers at the University of New Mexico had already identified it as Martian based on its oxygen isotopes, which serve as geochemical fingerprints for different planetary bodies. In this case, the researchers matched the meteorite’s oxygen isotopes to those seen in other Martian meteorites. Teghaza 001 appeared to be a shergottite which is the most common class of meteorite from the Red Planet. As an expert in planetary samples, Liu has seen plenty of those, but she decided to take a peek, anyway.
At the very least, there were odd textures and unusual minerals she hadn’t seen before. Liu and her colleagues discovered zircon crystals in Teghaza 001, which record clues to a rock’s formation and can be used by geologists to precisely age-date a sample. Further analysis revealed when Teghaza 001 formed and when certain changes, like water alteration, occurred.
Caltech coauthor Francois Tissot helped the researchers utilize a novel age-dating method pioneered by his team. Compared with bulk-analysis techniques, where a sample is entirely dissolved and analyzed, Tissot’s in-situ rubidium-strontium age-dating used a piece of Teghaza 001 that was smaller than a fingernail, analyzing single mineral grains on its surface. Besides its extreme precision and speed, the technique preserves rare samples like Martian meteorites for future studies.
“Right now, we are one of very few labs in the world able to perform this kind of age-dating, and the first to date such an ancient Martian meteorite,” Tissot said. “Our hope is to pave the way for dating even more Martian meteorites, or samples returned from

clusters.title_hint: Vega Island Frozen in Fright

sources.title: Vega Island Frozen in Fright
sources.text:
Shrouded in ice in the lonely Weddell Sea, Vega Island is an eerie sight to behold. On this speck of land east of the Antarctic Peninsula, ice, rock outcrops, and glacial moraines combine to create the appearance of a smirking skull in profile looking toward Devil Island.
These images show Vega Island’s creepy countenance at the start of austral autumn (left) and in spring (right). They were acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on March 22, 2025, and October 10, 2026, respectively. (Clouds obscured the island in March 2026.) A nunatak jutting out of the ice has the appearance of an eye socket, a lateral moraine forms a mouth, and Bahía del Diablo (Devil’s Bay) Glacier constitutes a jawbone. In the March 2025 image, a layer of snow coats the ice, which is typical of the region’s wettest month. That contrasts with the October 2026 image, when snow is absent from large areas and darker ice surfaces are visible.
Above-average temperatures in winter 2026—particularly in June—were partly responsible for so much bare ice in October, said glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College. The ice exposed on Vega and nearby islands indicates limited new snow accumulation over the winter, further reduced by sublimation and wind scouring, he said. “The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.”
The melt season ahead may also be more trick than treat. Bare ice is darker than snow and absorbs more solar energy, meaning that melting is poised to speed up as the days grow longer and warmer. “Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run,” Pelto said. “When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.”
The first comprehensive mapping of Vega Island’s ice was aided by Landsat imagery. In a study published in 1982, scientists described the island’s four ice caps with protruding rocky cliffs and outlet glaciers. They leveraged early Landsat observations along with aerial photos and topographic maps to catalog 29 glaciers on Vega.
Of those glaciers, Devil’s Bay Glacier has been closely monitored since the austral summer of 1998-1999, with researchers measuring an overall decline in its mass. Satellite images acquired in recent decades show ice loss from other glaciers on the island as well, with increased areas of exposed bedrock.
Long before scientists began tracking its glaciers, Vega was a bright spot in a tale of terror born out of early exploration of the area. The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901-1903 set out to study the geography, geology, climate, and wildlife on and around the eastern Antarctic Peninsula. The party became split into three groups during their explorations, isolated for a winter in different locations. Adding to the horror, they lost their ship to the pack ice. Cape Well-met, as it would come to be known, off the “forehead” of the Vega Island skull, was the site of a happy reunion of two of the groups in spring 1903. Soon thereafter, an Argentinean expedition rescued the survivors of the ordeal.

clusters.title_hint: November’s Night Sky Notes: Light-Day Away

sources.title: November’s Night Sky Notes: Light-Day Away
sources.text:
2 min read
In 1977, NASA launched twin spacecraft Voyager 1 and 2, taking advantage of a once-every-175-year planetary alignment of the four largest planets in our solar system: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Using six gravity assists between them, this Grand Tour gave us up-close views of the gas and ice giants, including several moons. By the 1980s, the two probes went their separate ways at Saturn. As Voyager 2 continued toward Uranus and Neptune, Voyager 1 grabbed one more portrait of the solar system (excluding Mercury and Mars), including a final image of the pale blue dot we call home.
“Hello from the children of planet Earth.”
Every good road trip needs some music to match. In this case, each craft carries the Golden Record, a 12-inch phonograph record with spoken greetings in 55 languages, 27 musical tracks, 116 images, and other sounds from Earth. Each record is protected by an outer cover featuring etchings showing our Sun’s location relative to 14 pulsars, along with instructions on how to play it. The design used various metals to protect the information encoded from space radiation: the record used copper and gold plating, and the cover used aluminum. The cover was electroplated with an ultra-pure sample of the isotope uranium-238. Uranium-238 has a half-life of 4.468 billion years.
Did you know that a light-minute is a measure of distance, not time? In August 2012 and November 2018, Voyager 1 and 2 crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun’s solar wind meets the interstellar medium. Using NASA’s Deep Space Network, Earth communicates with both spacecraft and tracks each on its journey. At the time of this article, the Canberra antenna tracked Voyager 1 at 25.80 billion km, or just over 16 billion miles.
On November 18, 2026, 49 years after its launch, Voyager 1 will cross the one-light-day mark, 16.1 billion miles from the Sun. You may have heard the term light-year in your favorite sci-fi movie or show, or when stargazing and referring to an object outside of our solar system. This video best demonstrates the different distances between the inner solar system, outer solar system, and beyond, using light measurements. Additionally, track each Voyager spacecraft here.
You can get a real understanding of what a gravity assist might be like with our Gravity Assist activity and learn what it’s like to measure a “light minute” with our Measuring a Kid Minute activity guide!

sources.title: A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System
sources.text:
Earlier this year, sources tell WIRED, a contractor caused a security incident at the Department of Defense by connecting a secure centralized system used by multiple intelligence agencies to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding agent. It appears that the agent used by the contractor, who is employed by the global consulting firm Accenture, then sent information about the DOD system, including login credentials, to a high-risk, third-party website.
The centralized system contains controlled unclassified information (CUI), which is considered sensitive and not to be released to the public without review. CUI can include information about critical infrastructure, nuclear submarine propulsion, and vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. Additionally, security experts say, access to the system could allow for the exploitation of even more sensitive ones.
“It puts all the data that’s in there at risk,” says a source aware of the incident, who requested anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the press. If the third-party software was compromised, “there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm.”

sources.title: What to Know About China’s Top-Secret Spaceplane
sources.text:
A winged Chinese spacecraft bearing a strong resemblance to the US military’s X-37B spaceplane was photographed in orbit by a passing US-owned commercial satellite in 2024, and we finally have the image.
The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays. In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the US Space Force.
The photo was taken by a commercial imaging satellite owned by a company called Vantor, known as Maxar in 2024. Vantor is one of several companies that provide reconnaissance imagery of locations around the world to the US military and US intelligence agencies. The same Earth-imaging satellites can point their telescopes at objects in space.
Lower-resolution views of a Chinese spaceplane showing the vehicle’s general shape were publicly available before the Defense Intelligence Agency assessment. A US Space Force official revealed Maxar’s observation at a 2024 conference in South Korea, but the Pentagon did not release the full-resolution image to the public until Monday, when it appeared in an unclassified DIA assessment of threats to the United States in space.
Catch and Release
The DIA report doesn’t reveal much new about what the Chinese spaceplane does in orbit. China has launched four spaceplane missions since 2020, with durations of up to nine months. The fourth mission is in orbit today after launching in February. It is not publicly known whether China has one or more such spaceplanes in its inventory.
The Space Force has two X-37Bs flying in rotation, with the longest of their eight missions to date running two-and-a-half years from launch until landing. US officials have released photos of the X-37B vehicles, published information about their design and dimensions, and disclosed a handful of experiments they have carried into orbit. Most of the X-37B’s activities in space are classified.
Like the X-37B, China’s spaceplane lifts off inside the payload shroud of a conventional rocket, then operates as a satellite once in orbit. The spaceplane flies like a miniature unpiloted version of NASA’s Space Shuttle and reenters the atmosphere for an autonomous land runway landing at the end of each mission. Ground teams then refurbish it for another flight.
The “enhanced maneuverability” of spaceplanes makes them “more suitable for certain missions than traditional satellites,” the DIA said in its report. So far, the Chinese spaceplane has only flown in low-Earth orbit (LEO) at an altitude of a few hundred miles. One of the Space Force’s X-37B flights soared to an altitude of more than 24,000 miles before using aerobraking to set up for reentry and landing.
Spaceplanes like China’s and the X-37B can also deploy small satellites from their cargo bay. Most recently, China demonstrated an ability to catch an object in orbit, perhaps using a robotic arm. The vehicle now in space released a sub-satellite in June and recaptured it in July, then did the same thing again in August and September, according to an analysis of open source orbital tracking data by Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist who catalogs spaceflight activity.
A Fleeting Glance
The official name of the Chinese spaceplane is even a mystery. It is often called Shenlong in Western publications, citing reports from the 2000s about China’s development of a robotic spaceplane. Chinese state media only refer to the vehicle as Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, or CSSHQ, which means reusable experimental spacecraft, according to a fact sheet published by the Secure World Foundation.
The DIA did not disclose the exact circumstances of Maxar’s observation of the Chinese spaceplane, such as its timing, location, or distance, but Earth observations often use cameras to view other objects in space as their orbits intersect, an emerging field known as non-Earth imaging (NEI).
NEI allows commercial operators and government analysts to inspect satellites. This is especially useful for gleaning information about classified or proprietary satellite designs, extending a new avenue for international and corporate espionage to the high frontier.
The capability exhibited by Maxar and other commercial companies in the NEI field is distinct from the recent actions of some military spacecraft, such as Russia’s Kosmos 2612, which deliberately maneuvered to approach a US-registered radar imaging satellite earlier this month. Commercial NEI observations come from chance encounters, often at extremely high speed.
Pew-Pew With DEWs
The DIA’s assessment of space threats includes an update on China’s pursuit of anti-satellite technology, or “counterspace” weapons. The two teams are the most recent Premier League champions, with Arsenal dethroning Liverpool last season to claim their first title since 2004. Together with Manchester United, the third member of this alleged group trying to undermine City, the trio have won 54 league titles and finished runners-up another 44 times, making them the dominant forces in English football history.
Yet all of them would have won more titles during the past decade but for the might of City. And as the eight-time Premier League champions continue to fight to overturn last month's verdict from an independent panel that the club was guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over a nine-season period, anger is growing among City fans about the perceived part played by Liverpool, Arsenal and Man United -- all of whom play in red home kits, giving the group its name -- in their downfall.
City were found guilty of producing "sham contracts" and artificially inflating commercial revenue by over £830 million, with Premier League CEO Richard Masters saying the club "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade." One team cheated, and that team has won six of the past nine Premier League titles. Oh, and they're currently in first place this season. Sports require some version of arbitrary integrity for them to make sense -- we currently don't have that.
Perhaps, more importantly, we don't even have the illusion of integrity right now.
Manchester City look like the best team in the league but we all expect some big punishment to be thrown at them any day now. But as I wrote about last week, the idea that the Premier League was fair before Manchester City were bought by Abu Dhabi United Group -- or that everyone else is still operating across an equal playing field -- was itself an illusion.
Last season, Arsenal won the Premier League with an estimated payroll of about €219.3 million, while Brentford had the league's smallest estimated payroll at €62.9 million. Outside of Leicester City's magical run in 2015-16, the team that wins the Premier League is always one of the richest teams in the Premier League.
So, as we continue to grapple with the meaning of what we've watched over the past decade, I wanted to look back on everything we've seen in a slightly different way: Who got the most out of what they spent? If everyone had roughly the same resources, who would've dominated the Premier League and who would've sunk to the bottom of the standings?
How we created the rankings
For this list, I looked at the last 10 full Premier League seasons, and I chose the 20 teams that played the most matches. Then, I gathered spending data from FBref, which has estimated wage data for every club, and Transfermarkt, which is the best public source for transfer spending data.
From there, I calculated the average total spending for every club in the seasons they competed in the Premier League. That total is just a combination of their average annual roster payroll and their average annual net transfer spending.
Finally, I took the total spending for each team and divided it by the number of points won in the Premier League standings -- a win being worth three points, a draw worth two.
That gives us the final metric to sort this list: millions of Euros spent per point won.
We'll start with the most efficient teams topping the list -- the teams that could shoot up the table if they were allowed to spend more money -- and, we'll continue down until we find the most wasteful teams that spent the most for the points they got.
1. Brentford: €1.2 million per point
We'll start with a graph that shows the relationship between average spend and points:
As you can see, there have been basically two Premier Leagues: one filled with teams that spend somewhere between €60 and €160 million on player costs, and then another with the teams that spend more than €200 million.
Brentford are the absolute bottom for total spending, but they're ninth in points won. If you look at the trend line, you can see that we'd expect a team with Brentford's spending to win something like 41 points per season but they've won about 51 points per season -- a 24% increase on expectation.
That, my friends, is what a willingness to embrace a new approach can get you. Brentford are the Premier League's "Moneyball" club.
They're run by a professional sports bettor who established proof of concept when he first bought floundering FC Midtjylland in Denmark and turned them into a Champions League team. Then he took over his boyhood club and got them promoted to the Premier League, where they finished ninth last season and currently sit sixth.
How best to describe what makes Brentford such a great club? They understand risk better than anyone else in the world: with how they hire managers, how they make tactical decisions, and how they acquire new players and depart from old ones.
This chart sums it up:
They know that most shots aren't going in, so what do they do to move the odds in their favor? They take higher-quality shots than everyone else, and they concede lower quality shots than everyone else.
Lastly, this isn't a case -- at least, not yet -- of an owner using data to spend less money on his team. Per Deloitte's most recent accounting, Brentford put 75% of their revenue back into wages. The average among the Premier League's so-called Big Six? 56%.
So, this is what it all comes down to: If Brentford had been allowed to spend as much money as, say, Manchester City, they'd be Premier League champions by now.
2. Bournemouth: €1.7 million per point
Bournemouth, too, are unafraid to do things differently.

sources.title:
How to Detect Financial Fraud Patterns
with Knowledge Graphs: A Production
Guide
sources.text:
Most anti-fraud architectures in enterprise payment workflows evaluate transactions in isolation.
When an invoice arrives, an automated rules engine checks it against static thresholds. It checks whether the dollar amount falls within normal limits, whether the vendor is on an approved vendor list, and whether the submitting IP address looks familiar. If the individual attributes look plausible, the payment clears.
The problem with this approach is structural. Sophisticated fraud schemes like money mule rings, circular invoicing loops, and vendor collision rarely produce transactions that alert individual thresholds. A shell company invoicing $4,800 to stay under a $5,000 dual sign-off threshold looks completely fine in isolation. But when 25 seemingly independent vendors all route disbursements to the same bank account, the coordinated pattern starts to become clear.
You won't find the warning in the attributes of an isolated transaction. It lives in the topology of the payment network.
In a relational database, tracing these multi-entity relationships requires recursive cell joins across tables of vendors, invoices, payments, and bank accounts. But as tables grow into millions of rows, deep path traversals quickly degrade query performance. Graph databases solve this by storing relationships as first-class, index-free adjacency pointers, turning multi-hop traversals into constant-time lookups.
In this tutorial, you'll explore the architecture of an end-to-end relational fraud detection pipeline built on Neo4j. You'll see how to model financial entities as a graph, precompute derived edges to optimize query latency, and write parameterized Cypher queries to uncover five core procurement fraud schemes.
The complete reference implementation is available in the fraud-detection-knowledge-graphs repository.
In accounts payable pipelines, risk checks typically operate on isolated records:
# Transaction-level view — nothing suspicious
transactions = [
{"vendor": "Alpha Corp", "amount": 5200.00, "date": "2025-08-01"},
{"vendor": "Beta LLC", "amount": 4800.00, "date": "2025-08-02"},
{"vendor": "Gamma Inc", "amount": 5100.00, "date": "2025-08-03"},
]
# All amounts within normal range ($1K–$15K). All vendors valid.
# Dates are sequential. Nothing triggers any rule.
When you map those same records to an interconnected graph, the hidden structure becomes clear right away:
# Graph view — all three vendors pay to the same account
connections = {
"ACC-MULE-001": ["Alpha Corp", "Beta LLC", "Gamma Inc"],
"ACC-0042": ["Delta Corp", "Epsilon LLC"],
"ACC-0099": ["Zeta GmbH"],
}
# ACC-MULE-001 receives from 25+ vendors. That's a money mule ring.
# The convergence is the red flag.
The underlying data hasn't changed. But when you evaluate transactions within an entity graph, the coordinated funnel stands out.
In a relational database, connecting these dots requires multiple joins across separate table. In a knowledge graph, the connections are stored directly as edges connecting nodes, which allows you to query them in a single traversal.
| Pattern | What It Is | What Traditional Tools Don't Catch |
|---|---|---|
| Duplicate Invoices | Same invoice and vendor, near-identical amount, close dates | Exact match misses slight variations |
| Circular Rings | Vendors invoicing each other in a closed loop | Each invoice looks legitimate alone |
| Money Mule Rings | Many vendors funneling to one controlled account | No single payment is anomalous |
| Vendor Collusion | Independent-looking vendors sharing underlying attributes | No cluster detection across entities |
| Payment Anomalies | Invoice approved by someone outside their department's authority | Role-based checks pass, context checks don't exist |
A knowledge graph doesn't replace rules engines or ML models. But it does fill the gap they can't reach: relationships.
To follow along with this tutorial, you'll need:
Before running fraud queries, you need to structure your data into a cohesive property graph. The reference dataset models six entity types commonly found in financial systems:
| Entity | Key Properties | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Vendor | tax_id, name, country, city | Who issues invoices |
| Invoice | invoice_id, amount, date, category | What was billed |
| Payment | payment_id, amount, date | What was paid |
| BankAccount | account_id, routing_number, bank_name | Where money went |
| Employee | employee_id, name, department | Who approved |
| Organization | org_id, name, departments | Structural hierarchy |
The base relationships form a bipartite payment network:
(Employee)-[:APPROVED]->(Payment)-[:LINKED_TO]->(Invoice)-[:ISSUED_BY]->(Vendor)
|
v
(Payment)-[:PAID_TO]->(BankAccount)
Real-world financial datasets are difficult to access because of privacy and regulatory restrictions. Using synthetic data allows you to inject known fraud patterns and systematically verify that your detection queries find them.

You likely use cloud services every day. When you check Gmail, join a Zoom meeting, or message your team on Slack, you use cloud-hosted software.
But you don't manage the servers it runs on or maintain the underlying infrastructure. You simply sign in and get to work. This is called Software as a Service (SaaS), and many people use it for years without knowing the term.
SaaS is just one of three major cloud service models. The other two, Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) and Platform as a Service (PaaS), give you different levels of control over the infrastructure and software you build. Understanding how these models differ will help you make sense of cloud engineering concepts and choose the right approach for your projects.
In this article, we'll break down IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, explain what you manage and what the cloud provider handles in each model, and learn how to choose between them for a real project.
By the end of this article, you'll be able to:
You don't need any cloud experience to follow this article. If you know what a computer, a server, and the internet are, you have everything you need.
If you're new to the cloud, read my article What is the Cloud and Cloud Computing? first. It explains what the cloud is and how it differs from running your own hardware, and this article builds on that foundation.
Cloud computing is a model that lets you use computing resources, such as servers, storage, and networking, on demand over the internet. YOu pay only for what you use.
These resources sit in data centres that are owned and run by cloud service providers, or CSPs for short. The best-known CSPs are Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud.
This is just a short recap to make sure you understand the key concepts. My article above covers it in full if you want or need more info.
Before the cloud, most organisations ran their systems on-premises. On-premises means the hardware sits in a building the organisation owns or rents. This could be a server room in their office, with its own staff looking after it.
In this setup, you're responsible for everything. This includes buying servers, setting up the network, installing and updating software, and keeping the room powered and cool.
For example, if a small business wanted to launch an online shop, it would need to buy a server, install the software, and pay someone to keep it running. If the shop grew faster than expected, it would need to buy more hardware.
The cloud moves some of that work to the provider. The physical servers still exist, but someone else owns and maintains them, and you rent what you need.
What differs from one cloud service to the next is how much of the work the provider takes on for you. The cloud service models describe this, and there are three main ones:
So a cloud service model describes how the work is split between you, the customer, and the provider, that is which parts of the system you manage and which parts the provider manages for you.
The shared responsibility model defines which parts of a cloud system the provider manages and which parts you, as the customer, manage. To understand it, you first need to see the parts that make up a running application.
A computing stack is the set of layers that work together to run an application. Each layer depends on the ones beneath it. From the bottom up, we have:
AWS describes the split as security “of” the cloud and security “in” the cloud. The provider manages the security of the cloud. This covers the data centres, physical hardware, physical network, and the virtualisation layer.
But security in the cloud is the customer's job. It covers what you put into the cloud and how you configure it. This includes your data, your users and their permissions, and the settings of the services you use.
Infrastructure as a Service is a cloud model where the provider gives you the basic building blocks of computing. This includes virtual servers, storage, and networking.
With IaaS, you request a virtual machine from the provider. You choose how many CPUs and how much memory it has, which operating system it runs, and which network it connects to. Within minutes, the VM is running, and you can connect to it.
From that point, the server is yours to manage. You install your software, apply operating system updates, configure the firewall, and keep your application running.
Before IaaS, getting a new server meant ordering hardware and waiting weeks for installation. With IaaS, the same server is ready in minutes, and you can delete it when you no longer need it.
Just remember: IaaS removes the hardware burden, but it doesn't remove the server burden.
With IaaS, you usually pay for each hour or second a server is running, plus the storage you keep and outbound data transfer.

Marketing has always involved wrangling lots of data. Before digital marketing, businesses had to track sales, customer purchases, coupon redemptions, store traffic, and survey responses to understand what their customers wanted.
And while digital marketing didn't invent marketing analytics, it dramatically increased the amount of information out there.
Today, almost every interaction can produce data. A person might see an advertisement, click it, visit a website, read an article, subscribe to an email list, open several emails, add a product to a shopping cart, leave the website, return through a search engine, and eventually make a purchase. And every one of those interactions can potentially become a data point.
For a marketer, this creates an incredible opportunity. It also creates a problem: having more data doesn't automatically result in better decisions.
A company can have hundreds of thousands of customer records and still not know which customers are most valuable. A marketing team can have dozens of dashboards and still struggle to answer a simple question such as, "Which campaign should we invest more money into?"
This is where programming becomes useful. Python gives marketers a way to work with data programmatically. Instead of manually opening spreadsheets, copying formulas, filtering rows, and creating the same report every week, you can build reusable processes that perform those tasks automatically.
More importantly, Python allows you to go beyond simple reporting. You can use it to investigate customer behavior, discover patterns, perform statistical analysis, create predictive models, automate workflows, and build systems that continuously transform raw marketing data into useful information.
That doesn't mean every marketer needs to become a software engineer. It just means that programming can become another tool in a marketer's toolbox and this tutorial explains how.
You don't need to be an experienced programmer or marketer to use this book, but a few basics will make the examples easier to follow.
You can follow the book using sample data. You don't need access to a company's private customer data or paid marketing APIs. If you use real data, make sure you have permission to access it and avoid exposing personal or confidential information.
This book focuses on three major ideas:
You'll begin with Python fundamentals and gradually move into more advanced applications.
By the end, you'll build a marketing intelligence system that combines many of these concepts into one project.
There's an important difference between learning Python and learning to use Python.
Learning Python means understanding syntax, data types, functions, loops, libraries, and other programming concepts. Using Python means taking those concepts and applying them to an actual problem.
This book focuses heavily on the second approach.
You'll still learn Python fundamentals, but the examples will consistently connect those fundamentals to marketing.
Instead of simply writing:
x = 10
y = 20
print(x + y)
we'll work with things like:

campaign_spend = 7350
remaining_budget = campaign_budget - campaign_spend
print(remaining_budget)
The programming concept is the same, but the context is different.
That context is what makes the skill useful.
Python doesn't know what a campaign is or what a customer is. And it doesn't know whether an advertisement is successful. Python simply processes the instructions you give it.
That means your first job is learning how to communicate with the computer.
Fortunately, you don't need to learn everything about Python before you can start working with marketing data. But you do need a practical foundation.
Programming can initially seem intimidating because computers are extremely literal.
If you tell a person: "Calculate how much money we have left from the campaign budget," they can probably figure out what you mean.
A computer needs explicit instructions. You need to tell it which values to use and which operation to perform.
For example:

remaining = budget - spent
print(remaining)

2650
The computer didn't need to understand marketing. It simply followed the instructions.
This is the basic relationship between you and a programming language.
You provide instructions, and Python translates those instructions into operations the computer can perform.
One of the most important programming skills is learning to break a large problem into smaller steps.
Imagine a marketing manager asks: "Can you tell me which campaigns are performing poorly?"

sources.title: How AI-Powered Search Works: A Guide for Devs on AI Visibility
sources.text:
Searched worked in a familiar way for decades: you'd type in your query, get back a list of pages, and choose one to click on. Behind the scenes, Google would find the pages it thought you might want, rank them, and give you a list of options.
But AI-powered search is changing that experience. If you ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, or another AI system a question, you may not get a long list of links to check out. Instead, the system can interpret your question, gather information from different sources when applicable, and generate an answer directly.
This changes something important for websites and brands: what happens when there's no traditional ranking position to fight for?
This is where the idea of AI visibility comes in. Instead of asking only, "Where does my website rank?", businesses and publishers are increasingly asking a different question: "Does the AI mention us when someone asks a relevant question?"
That distinction may sound small, but it represents a major change in how information is discovered online. And it's what we'll explore here.
If you're trying to understand how a search engine and an answer engine really work, it comes down to how each handles information retrieval.
Traditional search engines crawl the web, catalog pages in an index, run ranking algorithms against a user's keywords, and display candidate URLs ordered by perceived authority and link equity. The final decision of what to actually click on and read remains entirely in the hands of the person asking the question.
AI search changes things up a bit. When a user enters a natural-language prompt, the AI model decomposes the underlying intent, identifies candidate information using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (an AI technique that improves the accuracy of LLM models) or its pre-trained parametric memory, reconciles conflicting viewpoints, and actively decides which resources or solutions to present.
The most critical takeaway is that ranking highly on Google doesn't guarantee an AI engine will mention you. In fact, an Ahrefs citation study analyzing thousands of prompts discovered that only about 12% of URLs cited by generative assistants like ChatGPT and Copilot actually ranked in Google's top 10 for the exact query.
While Google’s own AI Overviews pull more frequently from conventional search results, standalone conversational engines construct independent answer graphs. AI visibility doesn't really care about claiming a specific URL slot. What matters more is whether your brand (and its resources) shows up as part of the machine’s direct answer.
If you strip away all the marketing language, AI visibility represents the probability and quality of your brand’s inclusion inside a synthesized response. Evaluating it requires breaking down three distinct dimensions:
This distinction matters because mentions and citations don't always happen together. An AI model can freely recommend your product because it understands your brand as a recognized entity, but cite a third-party tech review site as its primary factual reference. On the other hand, an engine might cite your documentation to clarify an API standard without ever suggesting your company as a vendor.
In order to appreciate how the AI chooses entities to include in its search results, we need to explore how modern retrieval engines work.
Current systems don't use only matching algorithms. They also incorporate elements of semantic analysis (the process by which an AI or computer program interprets the real meaning and context of words), vector representations (a way of turning words, sentences, or data into lists of numbers so that computers can understand their meaning) and multi-source verification (the practice of cross-checking a claim or dataset across multiple independent and reliable origins to confirm its truth and accuracy).
After the user provides the prompt, the system doesn't treat it as a set of words to be matched with an index. Using dense passage retrieval and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), the engine translates the request into a high-dimensional vector embedding of the real semantic context. The system then searches candidate passages on the internet, analyzing them through a variety of signals:
Core Signal | What the Engine Evaluates | Why It Impacts the Response |
Semantic Relevance | Meaning, context, and vector proximity | Resolves the user's underlying intent rather than verbatim text. |
Information Density | Presence of hard data, statistics, and verifiable claims | Models favor text rich in concrete facts over vague qualitative descriptions. |
Attribution & Provenance | Citations and attributed external references | Transparent sourcing allows the model to ground its claims safely. |
Cross-Source Consensus | Corroboration across independent platforms | If independent review boards concur, models accept facts as the truth. |
Information Freshness | Recent timestamps and active updates | Ensures specs, pricing, and availability refl

sources.text: Aegis is a free, open-source Android app for two-factor authentication codes. It stores codes in an encrypted vault and supports encrypted backups, so you do not lose access if you change phones. Official link: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.beemdevelopment.aegis

clusters.title_hint: Google Lens

sources.title: Google Lens
sources.text: Google Lens uses the phone camera to translate text in real time, copy text from paper, identify plants and products, and help solve homework, for free. Official link: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.google.ar.lens

clusters.title_hint: Perplexity

sources.title: Perplexity
sources.text: Perplexity is an AI search app that answers questions in full sentences and lists the web sources it used, so you can check them. It has a free plan. Official link: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=ai.perplexity.app.android

clusters.title_hint: Project Gutenberg

sources.title: Project Gutenberg
sources.text: Project Gutenberg offers over 70,000 free ebooks, mostly classics in the public domain, to download or read online. Official link: https://www.gutenberg.org

clusters.title_hint: Open Library

sources.title: Open Library
sources.text: Open Library, a project of the Internet Archive, lets you search millions of books and borrow digital copies of many of them for free. Official link: https://openlibrary.org

clusters.title_hint: MIT OpenCourseWare

sources.title: MIT OpenCourseWare
sources.text: MIT OpenCourseWare publishes materials from thousands of real MIT courses for free, including lecture videos, notes, problem sets and exams. Official link: https://ocw.mit.edu

clusters.title_hint: Edraak — Arabic online courses

sources.title: Edraak — Arabic online courses
sources.text: Edraak is an Arabic massive open online course platform, an initiative of the Queen Rania Foundation, offering courses in Arabic. Official link: https://www.edraak.org

clusters.title_hint: Audit Coursera courses for free

sources.title: Audit Coursera courses for free
sources.text: Many Coursera courses from universities and companies can be audited for free, which gives access to the course videos and readings. The paid option adds graded assignments and a certificate. Financial aid can be requested on eligible courses. Official link: https://www.coursera.org

clusters.title_hint: Bitwarden password manager

sources.title: Bitwarden password manager
sources.text: Bitwarden is an open-source password manager with a free plan that stores unlimited passwords and syncs across unlimited devices. Official link: https://bitwarden.com

clusters.title_hint: Google Password Checkup

sources.title: Google Password Checkup
sources.text: Google Password Manager includes Password Checkup, which tells you if any of your saved passwords were exposed in a data breach, reused, or weak. Official link: https://passwords.google.com

clusters.title_hint: Zotero

sources.title: Zotero
sources.text: Zotero is a free, open-source tool to collect, organize and cite research sources, and to generate bibliographies automatically in many citation styles. Official link: https://www.zotero.org

clusters.title_hint: Wayback Machine

sources.title: Wayback Machine
sources.text: The Wayback Machine from the Internet Archive stores copies of web pages over time, so you can see old versions of a site or recover a page that was deleted. Official link: https://web.archive.org

clusters.title_hint: Downdetector

sources.title: Downdetector
sources.text: Downdetector shows in real time whether a service such as WhatsApp, YouTube or Instagram is down for many users, based on reports, so you know if the problem is on your side or not. Official link: https://downdetector.com

clusters.title_hint: Google Fonts

sources.title: Google Fonts
sources.text: Google Fonts is a free library of open-licensed fonts, including many Arabic fonts, usable in designs, websites and commercial projects. Official link: https://fonts.google.com

clusters.title_hint: Canva for Education

sources.title: Canva for Education
sources.text: Canva for Education gives eligible primary and secondary school teachers and their students free access to Canva's premium features. Official link: https://www.canva.com/education

clusters.title_hint: JetBrains free student licenses

sources.title: JetBrains free student licenses
sources.text: JetBrains offers free educational licenses for its professional programming tools, such as IntelliJ IDEA and PyCharm, to students and teachers. Official link: https://www.jetbrains.com/community/education
